name: After the Campaign
scope: What happens after funding: fulfillment, oversubscription hazards, the redesign-eats-the-raise arc

claims.claim_text: The most common failure pattern among crowdfunded hardware campaigns is a team that reaches roughly eighty percent of a working design, raises far more than its stated goal, and then has no plan for the remaining work; the excess funding converts an unfinished prototype into a production commitment the team is not equipped to meet.
claims.quote_verbatim: the entrepreneurs have gotten to the 80% point, get funded way beyond their goals, and then have no clue what to do beyond that
claims.speaker: SPEAKER_01
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: A substantial share of the incoming work at contract manufacturing and design-for-manufacture consultancies comes from campaigns that funded far beyond expectation and only then discovered they had committed to shipping tens of thousands of units.
claims.quote_verbatim: they've listed their little project on Kickstarter and gone, holy crap, now I've got to ship, you know, 50,000 of these widgets
claims.speaker: SPEAKER_01
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Campaigns routinely set a pledge price without a costed bill of materials and overhead, so a half-million-dollar raise can leave zero or negative margin once real production costs land. The pledge price is fixed at campaign close and cannot be renegotiated with backers.
claims.quote_verbatim: they might get the half million bucks from their campaign, but then they realize, geez, I'm not actually going to make anything out of this because I didn't leave enough margin
claims.speaker: SPEAKER_01
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Platform policy directs a creator who cannot deliver to refund backers, but by the time a team discovers it cannot deliver it has usually spent the raise on parts, tooling and redesign, making refunds practically impossible.
claims.quote_verbatim: what basically Kickstarter says, if you can't deliver, you should give the money back. But at that stage, they've spent the money and it's very difficult to give it back
claims.speaker: SPEAKER_01
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Crowdfunding places blame on the individual rather than the venture: because the campaign is a public forum with direct creator-to-backer contact, a failure to deliver becomes personal hostility toward the creator rather than the impersonal write-off of a failed company.
claims.quote_verbatim: the challenge with Kickstarter is people hate the person. They don't hate the project. There's not that separation
claims.speaker: SPEAKER_01
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Non-delivery persists indefinitely in the public record: a campaign that raised roughly eighty-six thousand dollars for a lock-pick product remained undelivered years later after the creator's health failed, with no mechanism on the platform to close the obligation out.
claims.quote_verbatim: the poor guy that did the lock picks. He raised something like $86,000 a few years ago and has just not delivered
claims.speaker: SPEAKER_01
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Campaign dynamics force an unrealistic schedule: backers will not fund a stated one-to-two-year delivery, so creators promise around three months. Combining that schedule with a team that has never built in volume, a budget with no contingency, and direct customer contact produces a structure predisposed to fail.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to set some reasonable delivery date before you – to get anybody to back your product. You can't say it's actually going to take a year or two. You have to say I'll give it to you in three months
claims.speaker: SPEAKER_01
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Scale risk runs in both directions for a hardware startup: the central question is whether a sudden surge of demand can actually be delivered, which makes a very large crowdfunding commitment a hazard as much as an opportunity.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't want to get stuck with the, uh, the, you know, like a huge, a huge buy-in from Kickstarter
claims.speaker: Zach Hoeken
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Hoeken Smith - Creative China Commorant

claims.claim_text: After design-for-manufacture work and a hundred-unit test build, reaching very large volume takes on the order of eighteen months. Promising backers delivery next month and then landing fifty thousand orders with a three-month schedule is not merely hard but impossible.
claims.quote_verbatim: No one that I've ever talked to has told me that once you do DFM months and make a hundred of them for your, your tests, that it takes more than 18 months to make very large quantity
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: Hardware has no equivalent of recompiling and no built-in distribution channel comparable to an app store, so a production commitment made to backers must be right the first time; setting backer expectations correctly is therefore part of the engineering task.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to be perfect when you go to production
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: Campaign planning should assume overfunding rather than exact funding. Money raised past the goal converts directly into additional obligated work, in one account roughly four times the effort originally anticipated, rather than into slack or profit.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have a Kickstarter and you're looking for some money, plan for getting more money than you asked for
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bart Dring

claims.claim_text: Deliberately capping the number of units a campaign can sell bounds the manufacturing risk and keeps the run within the contract assembler's spare capacity; uncapped success can crowd out the partner's other production and generate delays that must then be explained to backers.
claims.quote_verbatim: I don't want to have such a successful project that I'm affecting SparkFun's ability to build all their other cool products
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: Both undershooting and overshooting the funding target destroy campaigns: too little money leaves the product unbuildable, while too much triggers uncontrolled scope and hiring, and either path ends in non-delivery. Even established companies fail this way.
claims.quote_verbatim: either it's not enough as we've talked about to meet their goals, or it's too much and they go wild and then don't deliver and then they just implode
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: 3D Product Logistics

claims.claim_text: A smartwatch campaign that sought a hundred thousand dollars, equivalent to roughly a thousand units, raised about ten million dollars from some sixty thousand backers. A thousand units can be assembled nearly by hand; sixty thousand requires an entirely different manufacturing plan, and the team abandoned its pre-campaign offshore strategy in favour of local production.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a whole different game plan from going for manufacturing a thousand watches, which you can almost, you know, do, you know, almost by hand
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: A frequent post-funding failure is spending the raise on headcount: teams that land a large sum immediately hire a chief executive and marketing staff, a pattern accelerators and investor networks actively encourage, which consumes the capital that was meant to fund production.
claims.quote_verbatim: they get their million bucks on kickstarter and then they go out and they hire a ceo and they hire a marketing person
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Headless Units and Baseless Batteries - KiCad Kickoff Kopophobia

claims.claim_text: The archetypal delayed hardware campaign has built fewer than a hundred units before launching, and only after the campaign closes does it possess a real specification and an understanding of its manufacturing constraints.
claims.quote_verbatim: they had, you know, made say sub 100 of a thing and they went on Kickstarter, raised some money
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Dunham

claims.claim_text: A campaign locks a fixed pot of capital against rewards promised at a fixed price while the true unit cost is still unknown; any later cost discovery has nowhere to go, because neither the price nor the amount raised can move.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have a fixed amount of capital that they've raised on Kickstarter. Right. They've promised these, you know, rewards or products at a specific price. And they didn't really have their costs really down
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Dunham

claims.claim_text: The dominant cause of eighteen-month delays is that the raise is consumed by redesign rather than production. Teams finish with a manufacturable design and no cash left to build it, forcing a second fundraise from venture investors just to produce what backers already paid for.
claims.quote_verbatim: you see these campaigns that are going on, they're delayed for a year and a half. Even in cases where people aren't paying themselves and, you know, are putting their own money into it, the money is going into redesigning these products
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Dunham

claims.claim_text: Five hundred thousand dollars is not a large sum for a hardware product, and campaigns have gone bankrupt after raising it because the amount was still short of what the product cost to bring to production.
claims.quote_verbatim: you get 500K for a crowdfunding campaign and a lot of companies have gone bust because they didn't get enough
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: Campaign budgets typically multiply bill-of-materials cost by unit count and stop there, so a twenty-dollar part cost becomes a two-hundred-thousand-dollar plan for ten thousand units. Non-recurring engineering, tooling, core firmware work and legal costs are omitted, and these are the costs that break the budget.
claims.quote_verbatim: everyone really just looks at, you know, what their individual bomb costs look like. And they say, okay, well, I'm going to make this thing for $20. So, in order to make, you know, 10,000 of them, it'll cost me $200,000. In reality, there are tooling costs involved
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: The lump sum that arrives at campaign close is almost entirely committed: a half-million-dollar raise can be followed by nearly half a million dollars of purchasing to fulfil it, leaving a balance far smaller than the headline figure suggests.
claims.quote_verbatim: you do your Kickstarter and half a million dollars suddenly appears in your bank account and you feel rich and then you realize, well, I've got to spend five and almost, almost that amount on actually buying stuff
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Ludicrously High Frequency Interference

claims.claim_text: Campaigns commonly fail not for lack of funding but because the funding is insufficient relative to real manufacturing cost; manufacturing in China is not the negligible expense that budgets assume.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's also why a lot of the crowdfunding campaigns fail, you know, because they just, they get a lot of money, but it's not enough
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Use The Protection Circuit

claims.claim_text: The money arriving at once is the visible part of a campaign; the obligation behind it is to build, ship, supply, test and support every unit out of that same sum, and misjudging the ratio leaves the creator working the obligation off at a loss.
claims.quote_verbatim: then you realize that you have to actually build it and ship them and supply them and test them and then back them all for that money
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Your Mind Is The Tool

claims.claim_text: A multimeter campaign that raised on the order of six hundred and fifty thousand dollars across roughly two and a half to three thousand backers produced little profit once the work was done, and almost none measured as an hourly rate.
claims.quote_verbatim: But how much profit did I make in the end from that? I don't know. You probably have to ask my account, but it's probably not much
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Your Mind Is The Tool

claims.claim_text: A million-dollar raise buys roughly five people for one year before any manufacturing, so a campaign of that size is not profit; at best it leaves a going company rather than a cash surplus.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's five people if you're not building stuff or if you're not manufacturing. That's five people for a year
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: CAD courses and cross platform creation - Printing Propaedeutic Patterns

claims.claim_text: Because a campaign trades a fixed sum for rewards at a fixed price, buffer must be built into the price before launch; a common rule offered to creators is to double the price they first calculate.
claims.quote_verbatim: the experience of asking for a fixed amount of money in exchange for a fixed price on a reward
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Dunham

claims.claim_text: A published analysis of low-cost 3D printer campaigns identified a viability curve below which bankruptcy before delivery is certain, holding even when the creator and staff take no wages; a three-hundred-dollar printer campaign falls below it unless volumes reach thousands of units.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's this viability curve, and if you're under the viability curve, you are guaranteed to go bankrupt before you can produce your 3D printers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Wrong Hardware, Wrong Software - Fugacious Fan Funding

claims.claim_text: Stretch goals are analysed as actively harmful rather than merely neutral: each additional promised feature adds cost and schedule against a price already fixed, driving the campaign further below the viability threshold.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's suicide to add all these stretch goals and stuff like that
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Wrong Hardware, Wrong Software - Fugacious Fan Funding

claims.claim_text: Scope accretion through added perks and features is a characteristic collapse mode for crowdfunded projects; constraining the problem to a minimum working configuration first is the discipline that prevents it.
claims.quote_verbatim: they'll think that they can do this and this and they can add this and add that and, oh, and this extra perk, you know. We'll just add this functionality. And then it just, it all falls apart
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Pull The Trigger

claims.claim_text: Platform and payment fees remove roughly eight percent of a raise before anything else: about five percent to the platform and three percent to the payment processor.
claims.quote_verbatim: So Kickstarter takes a chunk of it for their percentage, which I think is 5%. And then Amazon takes 3%-ish
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: A fraction of pledged money never arrives because cards are maxed out, stolen or otherwise fail at collection, and a further reserve must be left with the payment processor against chargebacks, so the usable cash is below the fee-adjusted headline figure.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a certain amount of people's, like, their credit cards were maxed or their credit card got stolen during the month
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: The combined platform and payment-processing cut is about eight percent, made up of five percent platform fee plus three to five percent for payment processing.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's 5% Kickstarter plus 3 to 5% payment processor
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with David Kronstein (Tesla500)

claims.claim_text: Sales deferred until after a campaign avoid the platform's percentage entirely, which is a reason to route some anticipated demand to post-campaign direct sales rather than maximising the campaign total.
claims.quote_verbatim: in some ways I would like to do it later because then I don't have to pay Kickstarter's cut
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with David Kronstein (Tesla500)

claims.claim_text: Crowdfunding platforms differ in when funds are released. One Australian platform paid out as soon as the target was met and before the campaign closed, allowing board fabrication and packaging purchases to begin immediately.
claims.quote_verbatim: with Possible when I did the ruler, as soon as I met my target, the money started rolling into my PayPal account, right? This is before the campaign even ended
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Chris Becomes Self Employed - Quixotic Quitting Quaere

claims.claim_text: Kickstarter releases funds only after the campaign ends plus a further hold of about two weeks. Creators who cannot self-fund parts purchasing during that gap start manufacturing late, which is a structural contributor to late delivery.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got to wait until the campaign ends. Then you've got to wait two weeks. They put the money on hold for two weeks and then it comes through
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Chris Becomes Self Employed - Quixotic Quitting Quaere

claims.claim_text: Long-lead components must be committed and paid for before a campaign launches, in one case a four-thousand-two-hundred-dollar reel, because parts ordered after the raise arrives will not arrive in time to meet the promised delivery date.
claims.quote_verbatim: I just paid 4,200 bucks for a reel of bloody components because if I don't get them, I'll be screwed and won't be able to, to, to fulfill the campaign
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: Building a larger run than the backer count uses campaign cash to seed post-campaign inventory: with about twelve hundred backers, one creator built two thousand units to cover distributor orders in lots of two hundred and his own direct sales.
claims.quote_verbatim: I only had 12,000, 200, 1200 backers. Right. So, technically I only have to make, but then, you know, I've been through this before and I'm smart enough to know that people are going to want these after the campaign
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Chris Becomes Self Employed - Quixotic Quitting Quaere

claims.claim_text: Component prices sourced through Western distribution can run roughly forty percent above the Shenzhen market for the same parts, so a forty-thousand-dollar parts bill would be around twenty-four to twenty-five thousand dollars bought locally in Shenzhen.
claims.quote_verbatim: These parts aren't cheap. I'm not buying these from the Shenzhen market. It's 40% less
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Chris Becomes Self Employed - Quixotic Quitting Quaere

claims.claim_text: Crowdfunding audiences are consumer audiences: developer platforms and boards address a market a small fraction of the size, so a platform product will raise a small fraction of what a comparable consumer device would.
claims.quote_verbatim: I did not understand that Kickstarter really is about a, a, a finished device that consumers can use. It's not about selling platforms
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: Crowdfunded hardware can reach buyers without the safety and electromagnetic-compatibility testing that a conventional retail channel would require, because the platform sits outside the normal distribution gatekeeping.
claims.quote_verbatim: The crowdfunding route seems to be a bit of a loophole when it comes to safety and EMC testing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Full compliance and safety testing is uncommon among crowdfunded hardware, so a campaign that has completed it is distinguishable on that basis alone; the cost and schedule of that testing is one of the items omitted from typical campaign budgets.
claims.quote_verbatim: This is full compliance tested, safety tested. I mean, how many crowdfunding campaigns do that? Not many
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter

claims.claim_text: Compliance testing is run on a small pre-production lot, on the order of ten units sent to a compliance house, and the turnaround runs to roughly twelve weeks. Starting it before the campaign rather than after keeps regulatory approval off the delivery critical path.
claims.quote_verbatim: there are 10 units currently at the assessment. What's the, you know, the compliance house. Oh, right, right, right, right. That are doing all the compliance testing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Milling About

claims.claim_text: Fulfilment changes character between hundreds and thousands of units. A few hundred packages can be stamped and addressed by hand; a few thousand requires mailing houses, direct envelope printing and postage franking machines, and the per-unit seconds saved become the design problem.
claims.quote_verbatim: I could easily, you know, buy a couple of hundred stamps and ship a couple of hundred envelopes. Not a problem, right? Yeah. But now it's a couple of thousand. No, it's a totally different board game
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Troubleshooting, PCBs and LEDs - Quaintized Quich Quelling

claims.claim_text: A run of a couple of thousand packages falls in a gap where it is too large to hand-process and too small for mailing houses to want, mirroring the component-buying gap where a single reel forces distributor pricing rather than volume pricing.
claims.quote_verbatim: a couple of thousand might be too small a job for a lot of these mailing houses
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Troubleshooting, PCBs and LEDs - Quaintized Quich Quelling

claims.claim_text: Flat products can escape automated mail handling: PCB rulers matching the envelope width shot out of the die-cut holes in the envelope ends when fed through the machine upside down, and had to be glued to a cut cardboard sheet to restrain them.
claims.quote_verbatim: each one had to be, uh, glued down to a cut sheet of cardboard for starters
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Fran Blanche Version 3

claims.claim_text: Fulfilment of a low-value item to a few thousand backers consumed months of a creator's time, which is a cost that does not appear in a bill of materials but dominates the schedule for cheap, high-count rewards.
claims.quote_verbatim: I spent months handling that, just trying to ship out these bloody rulers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Fran Blanche Version 3

claims.claim_text: Backer address collection was not a platform feature in the early years; creators had a single one-shot survey. At scale a team built its own web application so backers could enter and later amend shipping details, since manual address changes are only tractable at around a thousand backers.
claims.quote_verbatim: Kickstarter didn't even have a mailing address feature. They had this one, like you had one time you could send out a poll
claims.speaker: Andrew Witte
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: The backer survey can be issued only once, so an error in the survey or a wrong address supplied by a backer cannot be corrected through the platform. The exported data itself is usable, downloadable repeatedly as CSV and segmentable by reward tier and shipped status.
claims.quote_verbatim: Apart from the fact that you can only run it once, right? Yeah. Right. So if you goof it up and or somebody sent you the wrong address, they can't just update it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Manufacturing By Wire And Skipping Testing - Calefacient Cuculine Cash

claims.claim_text: Failing to subsidise international shipping is a pricing error discovered after launch. An oversized two-package shipment, a metre-long rolled surface in a tube plus a boxed unit of glasses and peripherals, made European delivery particularly expensive.
claims.quote_verbatim: a misstep on our part was not subsidizing shipping to Europe
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: Shipping volume has a worst-case middle band: too much to handle casually, too little to justify automating, and packing a single order costs about as much handling time as packing ten.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's really bad to be in that middle zone where you're shipping not quite enough to have everything automated, but not so little that you just give up on it
claims.speaker: Scott Driscoll
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Driscoll - Impacable Interdisciplinary Inventor

claims.claim_text: An online hardware business is predominantly a logistics operation; at a large open-hardware retailer the physical build-out is essentially all shipping, and high-volume online sales is itself the hard part rather than an afterthought.
claims.quote_verbatim: Almost every internet business is, is a huge logistics business
claims.speaker: Ryan O'Hara
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan O'Hara - Keyed, Kerfed Kapton

claims.claim_text: Post-design effort can exceed design effort by several times: a product taking twenty hours to develop and debug can take a hundred hours to ship and to optimise logistically.
claims.quote_verbatim: The thing that took me 20 hours to develop and debug now takes me 100 hours to ship and optimize logistically
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: Once units enter international post the creator loses visibility and control while remaining the point of contact for backers; a weather-driven backlog at a single hub can strand shipments for weeks with tracking showing no movement.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've been checking the tracking. It's just sitting somewhere
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Compare and Contrast Tech Entitlement - Worldly Working Wonks

claims.claim_text: Courier pricing stacks surcharges on top of the quoted rate: a fuel surcharge that had risen to around thirty-seven to thirty-nine percent of the shipping price, plus an emergency situation surcharge above that.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's an emergency surcharge, which is the COVID thing. And then there's a fuel surcharge on top of that
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Trade Show or Conference?

claims.claim_text: Aggregated shipping platforms resell a pooled carrier account, giving a small shipper volume rates and letting a packer work orders without access to the storefront; overnight cross-country US shipping through such a service can run around forty dollars for a subscription of roughly ten dollars a month.
claims.quote_verbatim: I use a thing called ship station, which is just like a, it's like a shipping server
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Artisanal Crystals

claims.claim_text: Product weight determines the freight mode and therefore the schedule: light items such as rings can be air-freighted even in quantities of a few thousand, while heavy products must go by sea, which in turn forces regional fulfilment centres and pulls in sales-tax obligations in each region.
claims.quote_verbatim: stuff like the everyday calendar, which is an incredibly heavy product, it really scales up. So all of those have to go by boat
claims.speaker: Simone Giertz
claims.episode_title: Product Design with Simone Giertz

claims.claim_text: A multi-vendor product converts fulfilment into a convergence problem: with the instrument, the case and the probes coming from three different countries, each leg must be separately arranged and any one late shipment holds the whole delivery.
claims.quote_verbatim: The meter comes from South Korea, the case comes from China, and the probes come from Taiwan
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Year End, 2017

claims.claim_text: Running a launch through a crowdfunding platform rather than a self-hosted shopping cart is defensible on logistics grounds alone: the platform delivers names, addresses and backer contact as a structured export, which is materially easier to manage than five thousand orders arriving through a storefront.
claims.quote_verbatim: logistically, when you'll suddenly get, you know, 5,000 orders or something, it's much easier to manage if it's not on your shopping cart
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Alternate Info Sources

claims.claim_text: Nobody launches a campaign intending to become a logistics operator, yet fulfilment competence is what separates campaigns that deliver from those that do not.
claims.quote_verbatim: no one's starting a Kickstarter, no one's starting a startup and being like, I want to get into the depths of the shipping logistics, you know, they have to, and the best ones do, are really good at it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Mapping Out Nerdery

claims.claim_text: Taking money up front converts backers into a standing support load: a hundred backers at fifty dollars generates continuous enquiries about delivery that the creator has no standing to refuse.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you've got 100 people signed up to this thing and they've all given you your 50 bucks or whatever, they're going to be emailing you every day
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Adafruit, Chip heist, Hackerspaces - The Kit Conniption

claims.claim_text: Pre-selling removes schedule contingency. A self-funded first run can absorb a setback silently, whereas a funded campaign has already published a delivery date, so any problem becomes a public delay.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you run into any problems, you don't have any contingency time
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Adafruit, Chip heist, Hackerspaces - The Kit Conniption

claims.claim_text: The creator's obligation under a crowdfunding campaign is to state expectations clearly and to keep working toward them until product is in backers' hands; the corresponding disadvantage is that the money is taken before the obligation is discharged.
claims.quote_verbatim: With Kickstarter, you're responsible for clearly communicating your expectations. And you're responsible for endeavoring to meet those until you deliver products to people's hands
claims.speaker: Ian Danaher
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Daniher - Nascent Nonolith Numquid

claims.claim_text: Campaign structure forces commitments before the decisions they depend on: a mechanical engineer and material selection cannot be hired or settled until funding lands, yet the campaign must already state a delivery date. The consequence is that a large majority of campaigns run late.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can't get that person unless you get funding. And you can't get funding unless you do your Kickstarter campaign
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: Honest scheduling is penalised at funding time. A stated one-year delivery drove backers away, while an understated six-month promise followed by slippage would have raised more, which is the incentive that produces systematically optimistic campaign dates.
claims.quote_verbatim: Being very honest about timelines hurt us. Just people like, well, I don't want to wait a year
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: Understating the true budget to make a goal look attainable creates a trap: a production that genuinely costs five million dollars advertised at five hundred thousand leaves the team boxed in when it raises a million and a half and then runs out of cash mid-build.
claims.quote_verbatim: They have to set it at $500,000 and then they get painted in a corner when they only make a million and a half and then they run out of money
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: Undelivered obligations persist for years: a creator who raised about twelve thousand dollars still had roughly forty significant rewards outstanding more than two years later, having been absorbed by a demanding day job, with the design still incomplete.
claims.quote_verbatim: I took $12,000 from you people and I've delivered not really anything worth $12,000
claims.speaker: Jeff Roberg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Rowberg - Mini Module Master

claims.claim_text: Refunding backers and abandoning a project are separable decisions. Returning the money while continuing development as a personal project discharges the obligation without ending the work, and is available whenever the raise is not required to finish.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a difference between giving up and giving money back unless you need the money to continue the development
claims.speaker: Jeff Roberg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Rowberg - Mini Module Master

claims.claim_text: Refunds become mechanically hard with age: payment processors only permit refunds through their system within a limited window, so returning money two years after a campaign requires contacting and paying each backer individually.
claims.quote_verbatim: PayPal only allow you to do a refund after a certain amount of time
claims.speaker: Jeff Roberg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Rowberg - Mini Module Master

claims.claim_text: Publicly stating that rewards cannot be delivered and offering the money back resolves the ambiguity that otherwise accumulates around a stalled campaign, even where backers have not been complaining.
claims.quote_verbatim: when I finally sent that out, I felt so much better
claims.speaker: Jeff Roberg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Rowberg - Mini Module Master

claims.claim_text: Platform terms require a creator who cannot deliver promised rewards to make best efforts to refund backers, but the practical enforcement route through litigation is effectively unavailable to individual backers.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you cannot deliver your promise rewards, you will do your best to refund people their money
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Our Second Callin Show(ish)

claims.claim_text: A funded team may decide mid-development that the promised reward is not worth shipping and pivot to a later, more polished product, substituting the eventual product for the original reward. This is a documented outcome for teams whose objective was to build a company rather than to ship the specific promised item.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're not really going to deliver our original promise to our Kickstarter backers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Our Second Callin Show(ish)

claims.claim_text: A campaign converts normal mid-development direction changes into a perceived bait and switch, because backers feel they have bought the specific advertised product. A team that expects to change direction gives up that freedom by pre-selling.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you change gears a lot in the process, as inevitably happens in development, you get – there's a slight worry that you've kind of bait and switched them
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: Crowdfunding performs three distinct functions: it moves revenue forward from the point of sale to the point of design and parts purchasing, it market-tests demand before commitment, and it assembles a community invested in the product. A team that already has cash and a community gains only the market test.
claims.quote_verbatim: it basically moves money forward in time
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: A campaign creates a liability on the creator's books: raising a hundred thousand dollars means owing a hundred thousand dollars of goods, which is a different financial position from having raised the equivalent investment.
claims.quote_verbatim: Kickstarter actually generates some liability
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: When a pre-campaign validation batch fails to arrive, launching anyway makes the first production lot the test lot; in one case a planned forty-unit trial was replaced by a first run of four hundred and fifty units shipped to backers, raising the exposure by an order of magnitude.
claims.quote_verbatim: we were hoping to get those 40 units so that we could ship them out so, you know, people could have a play with it and give us feedback
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Debugger vs Printeffer

claims.claim_text: Same-day shipping on the day funds clear is achievable and is the result of buying parts and manufacturing before the money arrives rather than after it.
claims.quote_verbatim: I shipped that exact day. Well, I didn't ship them all, but I at least shipped the, you know, the early backers on the exact day
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: No More Naming

claims.claim_text: A campaign scoped around an already-working prototype, assembled from existing modules rather than custom boards, delivered every unit in under sixty days. The narrow scope, not the technology, is what made the schedule achievable.
claims.quote_verbatim: we did, it was successful and we delivered all the phones in less than 60 days
claims.speaker: Christina Cyr
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Christina Cyr

claims.claim_text: Post-campaign sales, not the campaign itself, can be what makes a product a business: an open-hardware radio tool raised about fifty-three thousand dollars against a sixteen-thousand-dollar goal from only 441 backers, and follow-on sales within a couple of months of delivery supported the creator full time.
claims.quote_verbatim: within a couple months of delivering my units to Kickstarter backers, I had enough additional sales, post-Kickstarter sales, that I was able to quit my day job
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: Choosing a build quantity above the backer count to reach a price break is a deliberate risk decision: roughly sixteen hundred backers plus a few hundred later orders justified a twenty-five-hundred-unit run, a moderate rather than extreme scale of exposure.
claims.quote_verbatim: we had a little over 1,600 backers on Kickstarter and then a couple hundred in our creators and we decided to go with 2,500 units because that, you know, economically made sense
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Dunham

claims.claim_text: A campaign can function purely as an aggregated volume buy that reaches a price break, with the same hardware available immediately at low volume for roughly twice the price; backers are trading delivery time for the volume price.
claims.quote_verbatim: the Kickstarter was largely to, to allow us to get down on price and then to just get this in a lot of folks' hands
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: A first-time hardware team that promised about two thousand keyboards worked through a hardware incubator, visited around a dozen keyboard factories in Shenzhen, and took bids from roughly half before selecting one; the difficulties began after that selection.
claims.quote_verbatim: we ended up promising about 2,000 keyboards to Kickstarter backers
claims.speaker: Jesse Vincent
claims.episode_title: Stories from Teardown 2019

claims.claim_text: For a first production batch of a new product, proximity beats unit cost: problems are certain, and a factory the creator can visit resolves them faster than a cheaper remote one. The assumption that everything is made in China does not hold for first batches.
claims.quote_verbatim: for the first batch, it's almost always better to, you know, do it somewhere where you can just walk down the street and see it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Josh Lifton

claims.claim_text: Europe's largest campaign at the time, which raised about two point three million pounds, ended in company bankruptcy with no backer receiving anything, showing that scale of funding is not protection against total non-delivery.
claims.quote_verbatim: it is Europe's biggest Kickstarter project. And it, and it folded like, and it, nobody got anything
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: 3D Product Logistics

claims.claim_text: Platforms will cancel a campaign after funding: a laser-razor project that had reached about four million dollars, among the twenty highest-funded to that point, was suspended for lacking a working prototype, forfeiting the platform's own fee on that sum.
claims.quote_verbatim: They suspended it based on the fact that it didn't have a working prototype
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Amazon Moves In, Dave Says Run

claims.claim_text: Campaigns have presented resold off-the-shelf hardware, an Alibaba router with stock firmware, alongside photographs of boards claimed to be the product of years of in-house development. Reselling an existing product is legitimate; misrepresenting its provenance in the campaign is what triggered the backlash.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're just buying an off the shelf router from Alibaba and just whacking already off the shelf firmware in it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Warming Up To IoT - Tendentious Thermal Tools

claims.claim_text: Non-delivering campaigns divide into deliberate fraud and competence failure, the latter being creators who produced a render, assumed a Chinese factory could simply be paid to realise it, and found the assumption false.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's a huge difference between a genuine scam from the get go that they just want to steal your money and not produce anything. And ones that are just clueless
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Funding New/Manufacturing Old Projects - Radical Robotic Requisition

claims.claim_text: Platform vetting does not scale with volume. Early campaigns waited days for human review; later a reported perpetual-motion campaign was returned as violating no guidelines, indicating checklist-based rather than technical evaluation.
claims.quote_verbatim: the Kickstarter is so huge now that they don't have the number of people to evaluate every campaign
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Use The Protection Circuit

claims.claim_text: Crowdfunding backers are not professional investors and do not perform due diligence, which is why non-delivery imposes losses on people who had no realistic means of assessing the risk.
claims.quote_verbatim: You should do your due diligence and know what you're buying into. But all the, you know, people out there getting sucked in on these crowdfunding campaigns, and nobody's delivering anything
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: B Plus Boards and D Minus Cities - Uneath Urban Ubication

claims.claim_text: A reward-based pledge is an order, not an investment. That distinction matters because mail-order rules elsewhere oblige a seller taking card payment to actually possess or be able to produce the product, an obligation crowdfunding sidesteps.
claims.quote_verbatim: the misconception is that you're investing in the company. You're not. You're simply placing an order
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Larry Sears - Hexagram Hardware Holism

claims.claim_text: The defining structure of a rewards campaign is that the full amount is collected at close while delivery may legitimately be a year away, unlike ordinary card sales which are constrained to ship within a short window of the charge.
claims.quote_verbatim: you get all the money up front and then you can take a year to actually ship if you want
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: We'll Believe It When We See It - Hiring Hypercatalectic Helpelp

claims.claim_text: The platform's public disclaimer of retail responsibility was the direct catalyst for competing platforms founded by people with manufacturing and e-commerce experience, on the premise that crowdfunding and e-commerce are different systems and cannot share a back end unmodified.
claims.quote_verbatim: Kickstarter had it had for us, it's seminal blog posts of, you know, Kickstarter is not a store. They were reacting publicly to all of these claims about, well, Hey, you know, where's my thing
claims.speaker: Josh Lifton
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Josh Lifton

claims.claim_text: A curated open-hardware crowdfunding platform can bundle the post-campaign work the creator usually fails at: fulfilment, marketing, and continued sale of the product after delivery, treating delivery as the beginning of the product's life rather than its end.
claims.quote_verbatim: So we do fulfillment. That's why I'm sitting in a warehouse. We do marketing. We actually sell the products afterward
claims.speaker: Josh Lifton
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Josh Lifton

claims.claim_text: Choosing a platform that also acts as a stocking distributor smooths the transition from campaign to ongoing sales, but does not remove the inherent difficulties of crowdfunding, which are independent of platform choice.
claims.quote_verbatim: crowd supply also can help you transition into distribution pretty well
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan Cousins

claims.claim_text: The dominant platform partnered with a distributor and a manufacturing consultancy to launch a programme aimed at preventing hardware campaigns from failing after funding, an acknowledgement that post-funding execution was the systemic weak point.
claims.quote_verbatim: Kickstarter is launching a program to help prevent hardware startups from failing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Milling About

claims.claim_text: The manufacturing-support programme is curated and requires a previous successful campaign, and in practice selects projects already prototyped and part-way to manufacturable, which is the opposite of the early-stage creator most at risk.
claims.quote_verbatim: looking at your project, right, something that's already been prototyped and is effectively halfway to being manufactured
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Mergers and People Acquisitions

claims.claim_text: A funded campaign attracts targeted solicitation from fulfilment and manufacturing intermediaries offering to handle production or shipping for a percentage of the raise, typically around two percent, contacted through the public campaign page and the creator's professional profiles.
claims.quote_verbatim: we'll take, you know, 2% of your Kickstarter funds and we'll handle everything. We'll get it manufactured and we'll, you know, or we'll ship it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Year End, 2017

claims.claim_text: After several campaigns funded on renderings alone, the platform required a real demonstrable prototype and banned product renders, and applied category exclusions such as home-improvement devices; the first rejections under the change pushed those creators to build their own pre-authorisation payment pages instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: now you can't start a Kickstarter campaign unless you have a real prototype you can show
claims.speaker: Andrew Witte
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: A self-hosted campaign that pre-authorises payment and defers collection until shipment shifts risk back to the creator and correspondingly raises backer confidence, though it requires an independent funding source to carry production.
claims.quote_verbatim: they were able to defer actually collecting the money until shipping, which probably helped bolster people's confidence
claims.speaker: Andrew Witte
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: The prototype requirement is enforced by only one of the major platforms, so campaigns rejected for lacking a working prototype migrate to platforms without that rule rather than being stopped.
claims.quote_verbatim: Kickstarter have new rules that say you must show a real working prototype. Otherwise, bugger off
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, IndieGoGo & Ignite - Jasperated Jimswinger Jobbery

claims.claim_text: Campaign funding follows an exponential decay with a late upturn: most money arrives in the first days from early backers, the middle runs nearly flat, and large press placements produce only small blips. Once early backers have pledged they do not return, so mid-campaign promotion cannot recover the curve.
claims.quote_verbatim: everyone warned us ahead of time that it's going to be depressingly slow in the middle
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: Average pledge sizes on consumer hardware campaigns of that era ran around two hundred and forty dollars, so total raise can be estimated as backer count times that figure when sizing a production run.
claims.quote_verbatim: the average backing is about $240
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Specialized and/or Open Source Test Gear and Dev Boards - Vacation Videography Vorboten

claims.claim_text: A live campaign functions as cheap market research: floating a proposed stretch goal to backers and being told it is unwanted avoids committing engineering work to a feature nobody wants, replacing paid focus groups.
claims.quote_verbatim: he was hoping to offer other streaming services as kind of like stretch goals within his campaign. And he floated this idea and everyone said, no, I don't, I don't need it
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Dunham

claims.claim_text: Crowdfunded hardware outcomes sort into three bands: a barely-funded one-off, a raise large enough to fund a team and become a full-time company, and a middle band with too much delivery obligation to handle alone and too little money to hire help.
claims.quote_verbatim: he called the middle one the pit of despair
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Ceramic capacitors & High end scopes - Kempt Kickstarter Kakorrhaphiophobia

claims.claim_text: A mid-sized campaign can force a creator to leave employment to fulfil it and then leave nothing behind once the units ship, since a rewards campaign funds a delivery obligation rather than an ongoing business.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you just sold a couple of thousand of your widgets and you went, oh, shit, I've got to deliver a couple of thousand, and then that's it, it ended, then, well, you're out of a job
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Open Source RC & Modelsource - Facinorous Financial Foulness

claims.claim_text: A crowdfunding campaign is an effective lead generator for an electronics consulting practice, outperforming a website and business cards; the cost of that marketing is that the promised product must still be delivered.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've gotten more consulting business out of the one crowdfunding campaign than pretty much anything
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan Cousins

claims.claim_text: Once low-volume turnkey assembly made working prototypes obtainable for a few hundred dollars, the funding rationale for a campaign weakened and publicity became the remaining reason to run one.
claims.quote_verbatim: What you need Kickstarter for is for the publicity, right? It's a publicity machine
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Art Of Staying Interested In Electronics - Exponible Electronics Ennui

claims.claim_text: A creator who intends to build the product regardless can set the funding minimum at a nominal amount, which removes the all-or-nothing threshold and makes the campaign a pre-order and marketing exercise rather than a financing gate.
claims.quote_verbatim: I put my minimum funding as $1 and the crowdfunding went much better than I expected
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: A standing rule among some hardware practitioners is to fund production from retained earnings rather than take backers' money, on the grounds that an outstanding obligation to deliver removes the freedom to change or abandon a direction.
claims.quote_verbatim: I spend my own money, do it, and then I don't owe anyone anything
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Callow Cough Coverups

claims.claim_text: An augmented-reality campaign raised a little over a million dollars from about three thousand backers and used it as first outside capital to begin hiring while still operating from a residence, an arrangement that became the limiting stressor as headcount grew.
claims.quote_verbatim: we did a Kickstarter campaign where we raised a bit over a million dollars and had, like, 3,000 backers on it. And then we took that money
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: Backers of a finished-looking consumer reward expect a finished consumer product, and receiving something that cannot be used out of the box is a delivery failure even when units have physically shipped.
claims.quote_verbatim: I bought a watch. And I could not turn it on and play with it out-of-the-box
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Is This A Show?
